content:
In what generality is continuous cohomology used in mathematics?

Mathlib now has docs#continuousCohomology and I am concerned about the definition after seeing a PR to FLT. Right now continuous cohomology in mathlib eats a group with a topology, a coefficient ring kkk with a topology, and a topological kkk-module with a GGG-action (which is not assumed to be continuous), and spits out a topological kkk-module. Cohomology is made using n-chains which are continuous in some curried sense.

For me several things are backwards here. In the example of continuous cohomology which I care about, we have a profinite group, a commutative ring and a module over that ring with an action of the group (no topologies assumed to exist on the ring and the module), and the continuity axiom is that stabilisers are open. Cohomology is then computed with locally constant functions.

Aha, people might say: "stabilisers are open" and "locally constant functions" is just a way of saying "continuous action with respect to the discrete topology" so what you want is somehow a special case of what is there. But there is an issue here. One definitely wants to look at Hn(Gal(Q‾p/Qp),Q‾p×)H^n(Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p/\mathbb{Q}_p),\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\times)Hn(Gal(Q​p​/Qp​),Q​p×​) (for example the computation of this group when n=2n=2n=2 is a deep result in local class field theory) and in this situation Q‾p×\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\timesQ​p×​ already has a completely natural topology coming from the metric and it is not discrete, however the Galois group acts and stabilisers are open anyway. Right now in order to write down this cohomology group in mathlib we will have to artificially put the discrete topology on Q‾p×\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\timesQ​p×​ and this smells bad to me. We do not actually have the correct topology on this object as an instance yet, but I would definitely not want to rule out putting the correct topology on this object in the future.

All this has led me to ask: what are the uses of continuous cohomology in mathematics beyond those which I know about? I talked to Richard Hill about this and he suggested that Pontrjagin duality was about continuous group homs to the circle and continuous group homs are an example of an H^1 in mathlib, but I didn't feel like this was a strong argument: it was not clear to me that it was helpful to think about this cohomological interpretation of Pontrjagin duality and this felt more to me like a coincidence.

I dimly remember as a graduate student attending a course by John Coates where E/QE/\mathbb{Q}E/Q was an elliptic curve and he was interested in H1(Gal(Q‾/Q),Tp(E))H^1(Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}),T_p(E))H1(Gal(Q​/Q),Tp​(E)) (the Tate module)$$ and he stressed that one had to be careful here because this HnH^nHn was not a derived functor, it was defined using continuous cocycles and coboundaries. Do people still use this kind of thing?

What should we be covering in mathlib? I don't have any objections to yet another cohomology theory. We have group cohomology, Tate cohomology and now this version of continuous cohomology which IMO is asking for too much topology on the algebra, maybe we just add "profinite cohomology" which is where a topological group G acts on a topology-free M with open stabilisers; this way we will be able to talk about Hn(Gal(Q‾p/Qp),Q‾p×)H^n(Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p/\mathbb{Q}_p),\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\times)Hn(Gal(Q​p​/Qp​),Q​p×​) without putting a spurious discrete topology on the module. Or am I fussing about nothing?

The union of Mathlib and the proetale lib of @Christian Merten and @Jiang Jiedong gives you access to both condensed cohomology and pro-etale cohomology. Of course nothing there will tell you that you can compute cohomology groups using cochains. But would it be an idea to add such a piece of API on top of those definitions? Would that help you?
In both cases you would also have to work a bit, either to make your objects condensed, or to replace your infinite Galois group with spec of a field, etc...
I might be confused but docs#continuousCohomology does take a topology on G and the cochains are indeed continuous with respect to that topology?

You're absolutely right, I completely missed this, I will edit. My point stands though -- it demands a topology on the module, and to recover the usual case of profinite topology the topology on the module has to be discrete whereas I give an example above where the natural topology is not discrete.

Aah -- the topology is not asked for in TopRep, that's where there's no topology. As I say, I'll edit.

TopRep does contain the data of a topology on the module. (Edit: I now realise you meant that it does not require the G-action to be continuous. Yes you are right.)

A way to get what you want easily is to make a constructor TopRep.mkDiscrete that takes in a module without topology with open stabiliser conditions and make the topology internally.
(and then develop API on top of this so that the internal discrete topology does not leak out)
I see. Yes I would be far happier with this than randomly putting the discrete topology on Q‾p×.\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\times.Q​p×​. Do you think that this is the way to proceed?
This has recently been refactored by @Edison Xie in #41144. IIRC his idea was exactly what Andrew is describing.

I am concerned about whether we are overengineering this. My question remains: what are examples of "continuous cohomology" in real mathematics which go beyond the case of GGG profinite acting on MMM with open stabilisers?
I think Edison was convinced by Richard, so his motivation was probably what you described above.

But I asked Richard this question and I was not convinced he had an answer (as I say he mentioned Pontrjagin duality but I think this is bogus).

I am rather hoping that there is an answer of the form "Tate carefully considered all this in the 1960s and wrote some papers on K-theory where the definition we have in mathlib really is necessary" (this might be the case)

One example is the absolute Galois group GQpG_{\mathbb{Q}_p}GQp​​ act continuously on Cp\mathbb{C}_pCp​. For any element x∈Cpx \in \mathbb{C}_px∈Cp​, having open stablizer is equivalent to living in finite extension of Qp\mathbb{Q}_pQp​. So indeed there are elements not having open stablizer. In addition to Hi(GQp,Cp)H^i(G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}, \mathbb{C}_{p})Hi(GQp​​,Cp​), one also wants to calculate Hi(GQp,BdR+)H^i(G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}, B_{dR}^+)Hi(GQp​​,BdR+​).

Oh marvellous! Are you clear on the definition of these objects? Is it definitely what we have in mathlib? Once someone convinces me of this I am going to be far less worried, and will be happy to adopt Andrew's strategy for forcing the discrete topology on a module which does not want to have it in general.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Oh marvellous! Are you clear on the definition of these objects? Is it definitely what we have in mathlib?

Yes, we have definition of these rings in Mathlib. The group action instance is not there yet, but its not very hard to implement.
Oh I know what the definition of the modules and the group action is, I am specifically asking about the definition of the cohomology groups. I don't understand mathematically what has been merged.

Example of what I don't understand: my guess as to what H2H^2H2 would mean is continuous cocycles G×G→MG\times G\to MG×G→M modulo continuous coboundaries (and I would not give the quotient a topology). But I think that what we have is something like continuous maps from G to the space of continuous maps from G to M with maybe some kind of compact open topology? And also our cohomology groups are somehow inheriting a topology. Is this topology meaningful? Do people studying Hi(GQp,BdR+)H^i(G_{\mathbb{Q}_p},B_{dR}^+)Hi(GQp​​,BdR+​) expect a topology on their cohomology groups and if so, do we have the right one?

i.e. my question has now changed from "can you give examples of continuous cohomology which are not profinite groups acting with open stabilisers" to "can someone reassure me that in the example which we now know where stabilisers are not open, our definition is correct"
Oh... Is the current definition correct..?

Well I did not want to ask that question before because my original question was "is this definition even useful". You have now given what looks like a good answer to this.

My guess is that the definition is OK. I am hoping that the fact that G is profinite means that the compact open topology on hom sets will somehow unravel to precisely the statement that the n-cochains being considered are precisely the continuous ones.
Are you looking for Homeomorph.curry?
So it may be wrong for a non locally compact group, and the question is now if we care about the cohomology of nonlocally compact groups.

By the way, I don't know whether we should equipped the cohomology group with the quotient topology.

I didn’t come up with any case where people actually used a topology on the continuous cohomology group. Perhaps someone else can find further examples where a topology on these groups is used.

Kevin Buzzard said:

I dimly remember as a graduate student attending a course by John Coates where E/QE/\mathbb{Q}E/Q was an elliptic curve and he was interested in H1(Gal(Q‾/Q),Tp(E))H^1(Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}),T_p(E))H1(Gal(Q​/Q),Tp​(E)) (the Tate module) and he stressed that one had to be careful here because this HnH^nHn was not a derived functor, it was defined using continuous cocycles and coboundaries. Do people still use this kind of thing?

I'm embarrassed to say that during math research, all of my knowledge on continuous cohomology are taken for granted. But I remember there are some classical references, e.g. Jannsen's 1988 paper Continuous etale cohomology, Nekovar's 2006 book Selmer complexes. At least they discuss the reason why choose such definition for continuous cohomology to some extent. There is a screenshot of contents of Selmer complexes:

Also, in Colmez's 1998 paper Theorie d'Iwasawa des representations de de Rham d'un corps local, the continuous cohomology of measures and tempered distributions on Zp\mathbb{Z}_pZp​ are related to Iwasawa cohomology via Shapiro lemma.

Here is a scary example. What is H1(GQp,Q‾p×)?H^1(G_{\mathbb{Q}_p},\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\times)?H1(GQp​​,Q​p×​)? Well by Hilbert 90 this is zero. But here is a continuous 1-cocycle: GQpG_{\mathbb{Q}_p}GQp​​ surjects onto Gal(Qp(ζp∞)/Qp)=Zp×↪Q‾p×Gal(\mathbb{Q}_p(\zeta_{p^\infty})/\mathbb{Q}_p)=\Z_p^\times\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\timesGal(Qp​(ζp∞​)/Qp​)=Zp×​↪Q​p×​ and this satisfies c(gh)=c(g)+gc(h)c(gh)=c(g)+gc(h)c(gh)=c(g)+gc(h) because it's a group homomorphism with Galois-invariant target. And this isn't a 1-coboundary because all 1-coboundaries are locally constant. Contradiction!
But the cyclotomic character is not continuous if you endow Q‾p×\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\timesQ​p×​ with the discrete topology (the image is infinite), so Hilbert 90 doesn't care.

Right, but my point is that (a) if mathlib ever endows Q‾p×\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\timesQ​p×​ with a topology, it won't be the discrete topology, and (b) (much more importantly) Jiedong is claiming that people study Hi(GQp,Cp)H^i(G_{\mathbb{Q}_p},\mathbb{C}_p)Hi(GQp​​,Cp​) where now Cp\mathbb{C}_pCp​ really does have the ppp-adic topology, so we seem to have the "continuous cohomology group" H1(GQp,Q‾p×)H^1(G_{\mathbb{Q}_p},\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\times)H1(GQp​​,Q​p×​) and "the continuous cohomology group" H1(GQp,Cp)H^1(G_{\mathbb{Q}_p},\mathbb{C}_p)H1(GQp​​,Cp​) in the mathematical literature with literally different definitions of "continuous cohomology" (the first being "obviously ignore the topology on the module, it's the topology on the group that matters" and the second being "obviously don't ignore the topology on the module", and my example proving that these are genuinely different objects). Right now mathlib has the second definition of continuous cohomology and I claim that at the very least this is a footgun.

It seems so, it's a bit ugly for formalization. Maybe your idea of profinite cohomology is the good solution:

  • it is more readable as one changes the "H" instead of changing Q‾p×\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\timesQ​p×​
  • it's a special case of continuous cohomology so the API is already there

This is not quite an answer to your question @Kevin Buzzard , but about something close: there is a definition of a group cohomology for Lie groups (and everything kinda works the same in the topological category, too) considered by Brylinski here: https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0011069, where the cochains are continuous (and smooth, in the smooth category) in a neighbourhood of the identity in the group.

And see also earlier work by Segal (published by him, but joint with Mitchison): https://dmitripavlov.org/scans/segal-cohomology-of-topological-groups.pdf with a review in section 4.1 of https://arxiv.org/abs/0911.2483

So this is used in a very different way to what you are used to, but it just a little different. I can't speak to how the two versions relate for the profinite groups and topological modules you are interested in, but I'm curious if any of this version is meaningful for you, or worthy for mathlib.

There are many things that can be said here, but maybe the most compact thing one can say is that Kevin’s example is a bit ad-hoc in the sense that Hilbert 90 is a statement about (pro)étale cohomology and thus the coefficients should have the spelling Gm\mathbb{G}_mGm​ rather than Qp‾×\overline{\mathbb{Q}_p}^\timesQp​​×.
And H1(GQp,Cp)H^1(G_{\mathbb{Q}_p},\mathbb{C}_p)H1(GQp​​,Cp​) is not spelt H1(GQp,G^a)?H^1(G_{\mathbb{Q}_p},\widehat{\mathbb{G}}_a)?H1(GQp​​,Ga​)?
I guess another question then is relating continuous cohomology in the mathlib sense to proetale cohomology in the mathlib sense.
